title: Machine or Robot?
description: A washing machine has motors, sensors and a computer inside. So why is it not a robot? One question settles it.

content.value: The Test
One question sorts almost every machine correctly. Does it change what it does, based on what it senses?
If the answer is no, and it repeats the same steps no matter what, it is a machine. If the answer is yes, it is a robot.
The washing machine
Press "Cotton" and it fills, spins, drains, then spins again. The same steps, in the same order, every single time.
It does have a water sensor and a timer. But they only tell it when to move on to the next fixed step. The plan itself never changes, so it is a machine.

content.want: A washing machine program dial or control panel, close enough to read the cycle names
content.alt: The program selector dial on a washing machine
content.caption: Every setting is a fixed list of steps. The dial picks which list runs, and that is all.

content.value: The robot vacuum
Put it in a different room and it cleans a different path. Move a chair and tomorrow's route changes. It builds the plan from what it senses, so it is a robot.

content.want: A robot vacuum mid-clean in a real room, ideally showing its bumper and top sensor turret
content.alt: A robot vacuum cleaner navigating a living room floor
content.caption: Same program, different room, different path, because it looks first.

content.value: Try it yourself. Same room, same starting point, one box in the way. Run the fixed program, then run the robot. Then move the box and run both again.

Same steps      Changes its plan
                  every time?     from sensors?

Washing machine       yes              no      → machine
Toaster               yes              no      → machine
Robot vacuum          no               yes     → ROBOT
Self-driving car      no               yes     → ROBOT
The tricky ones
Some machines sit right on the line. Arguing about those is the fastest way to really understand the test. Here are three worth arguing about.

A thermostat senses the temperature and switches the heater on or off. So it senses, decides and acts. Most people still call it a machine, because it has exactly one rule. If you called it the world's simplest robot, you would not really be wrong.
A factory arm welding car doors repeats one memorised movement forever, with no sensors at all. Most people call it a robot because it looks like one. By our test it is a machine in a robot costume.
A drone flying a route you typed in never looks around. Same answer: it is a very expensive machine. Give it a camera that makes it dodge a bird and it becomes a robot.
All three of these are machines

items.want: A wall thermostat, dial or digital, close enough to read the temperature
items.caption: It senses, then it switches. One rule, one output.

items.want: An industrial welding arm on a car production line, sparks visible if possible
items.alt: An industrial robot arm welding a car body on a production line
items.caption: Repeats one memorised movement, whatever is in front of it.

items.want: A consumer quadcopter drone in flight against open sky
items.caption: Flies the route you typed. Never looks around.

content.value: Shape is not the test. A machine can look like a person, and a robot can look like a hockey puck. Always ask the same question instead: does it change its plan from what it senses?
So what about remote control?
A remote-control car is not a robot, because you are its brain. The sensing happens in your eyes and the thinking happens in your head, both outside the machine.
That is worth noticing rather than treating as a failure. Plenty of real robots start out remote-controlled, and the brain gets moved inside them later. You will do exactly that in this course.
Your turn: twelve machines, two bins
Sort all twelve before you press check. Four of them are genuinely arguable. If you can explain why you put one where you did, you have understood the test.

content.prompt: The test: does it change what it does based on what it senses?
content.note: The hard ones: a factory arm with no sensors repeats a fixed movement forever, so it is a machine. A thermostat really does sense, decide and act, so calling it the world's simplest robot is fair.

cards.label: Drone that dodges birds it spots

content.value: Key takeaway: a robot decides for itself, using what it senses. If it runs the same steps no matter what, or if a human is doing the deciding, it is not a robot.

quiz.question: A drone flies a route you typed in and never changes it. Robot?
options: Yes, because it flies by itself
No, because it never changes its plan from what it senses
Yes, because anything that flies is a robot
quiz.explain: Flying by itself is not enough. It follows a fixed list of points, the same way a washing machine follows a fixed wash cycle.

quiz.question: A vending machine takes your money, checks the coin, and drops the snack you chose. Robot?
options: No, because the same steps run every time, whatever it senses
Yes, because it has a coin sensor
Yes, because it moves things around
quiz.explain: Having a sensor is not the test. Its coin sensor only confirms a fixed step. The plan never changes.

quiz.question: Your friend says a robot vacuum can't be a robot because it doesn't have arms or a face. What's the best reply?
options: They are right, robots need arms
Shape does not matter. Deciding for itself from sensors does
They are right, it is a vacuum and not a robot
quiz.explain: Plenty of real robots are boxes, discs or drones. What counts is whether it changes its plan from what it senses.

quiz.question: You drive an RC car around your room with a controller. Which box of the loop is happening OUTSIDE the car?
options: Neither, because it is a full robot
quiz.explain: Your eyes do the sensing and your brain does the thinking. The car only acts. Move those two jobs inside the car and it becomes a robot.

quiz.question: A factory arm welds the same spot on every car with no sensors at all. By our test, what is it?
options: A robot, because it is in a factory and looks like one
A machine, because it repeats fixed steps and senses nothing
Neither, because it is just a tool
quiz.explain: Everyone calls it a robot arm, and that is fine in everyday speech. But by the sense, think, act test, no sensing means no deciding.

quiz.question: Which change would turn a fixed-route delivery drone into a robot?
options: Adding a camera that makes it fly around obstacles it spots
quiz.explain: That completes the loop. It senses something new, decides, and changes what it does. Speed and paint change nothing.
